paras: The lynching of David N. Lee was the hanging of a young man by unknown parties on the Brake road near Holly Grove Church in Franklin Parish, Louisiana, in late 1882. A card left in his pocket blamed "hog meat," and the Lake Charles Echo reported that a mob had hanged him on mere suspicion of stealing hogs. The governor offered a reward for each member of the mob, and both papers that reported the killing condemned it.
Lee was a young man born and raised in Franklin Parish who left a wife and child; neither account states his race.

On a Saturday night between 10 and 11 o'clock, Lee left F. N. Abell's store for home with his brother John Lee and Purvis Roberts. Roberts turned off toward his own home, and Lee declined his brother's invitation to stop at John's house and rode on alone, the last time he was seen alive. His horse came home on Sunday afternoon with the bridle over the pommel, and neighbors began a search.

On Monday morning his body was found hanged to a tree about three-quarters of a mile from his home on the Brake road, 4 or 5 miles from Holly Grove Church. In his pocket was a card reading "Lee is dead, hog meat killed him; boys, go slow on hogs."

Esquire Dobyn summoned a jury, which found that Lee died "by hanging perpetrated by unknown parties." Neighbors who sat up with the body said there was not a pound of meat of any kind in the house, and the Franklin Sun reported "great indignation" in the neighborhood and the parish. A posse under the sheriff set out to arrest certain parties supposed to be implicated, and the governor offered $250 for the arrest of each member of the mob. No report of an arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The local Franklin Sun account, reprinted by the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe on December 2, ran under the headline "Mob Law in Franklin Parish" and called the killing a "dastardly deed." By pointing to the empty larder, the Sun cast doubt on the hog-theft charge implied by the card. On December 9 the Lake Charles Echo, while holding that some crimes deserved mob hanging, called "jerking up a man simply upon suspicion" of theft "an outrage and a disgrace to the state" and urged punishment of the killers. Neither paper mentioned Lee's race or the race of his killers.

bases: Lee was found hanged to a tree with a card about hog meat in his pocket, an inquest found hanging 'by unknown parties', and the Lake Charles Echo said he was hanged 'by a mob' on suspicion of hog theft (A1, A2).

Lee was hanged by unknown parties without legal process, and the card ('boys, go slow on hogs') and the Echo's report tie the killing to suspected hog theft (A1, A2); the Echo calls the killers a mob but no paper gives their number (A2).

The Franklin Sun account reprinted in the Ouachita Telegraph and the separate Lake Charles Echo editorial agree that Lee was hanged in Franklin Parish by unknown killers, the Echo adding the governor's reward (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Franklin Sun (local)
accounts.gist: Lee disappeared riding home Saturday night and was found hanged Monday with a card blaming 'hog meat'; an inquest found unknown parties responsible and neighbors said his house held no meat.

accounts.label: Lake Charles Echo editorial
accounts.gist: A mob hanged Lee merely on suspicion of stealing hogs, and the governor offered $250 for each mob member's arrest.

framing.detail: The Franklin Sun story ran under 'Mob Law in Franklin Parish', called the killing a 'dastardly deed' and stressed that no meat was found in Lee's house.
